policy_title: Meaningful and Binding Nature Targets ('Double Nature')
stated: Set meaningful and binding targets to stop the decline of our natural environment and ‘double nature’ by 2050: doubling the size of the Protected Area Network, doubling the area of most important wildlife habitats, doubling the abundance of species and doubling woodland cover by 2050.

source.quote: Set meaningful and binding targets to stop the decline of our natural environment and ‘double nature’ by 2050: doubling the size of the Protected Area Network, doubling the area of most important wildlife habitats, doubling the abundance of species and doubling woodland cover by 2050.

bearing_set.reason: Directly sets binding targets to halt environmental decline and expand habitats, woodland, and species abundance — a material effect on clean environment indicators including nature, emissions (via woodland carbon), and ecosystem health.

Binding statutory targets at this scale (doubling Protected Area Network, habitats, woodland) would require substantial, legally enforceable public expenditure — land acquisition, agri-environment payments, management contracts, enforcement — creating a material multi-decade fiscal commitment that moves the debt-path/funded-vs-borrowed indicator regardless of which funding mechanism is chosen.

membership_note: O6 is the primary bearing and is strongly positive; O12 is a genuine secondary bearing because 'binding' targets at this ambition level are not costless aspirations — they legally obligate delivery spending. O1 (housing supply) is plausible but attenuated: woodland expansion typically targets marginal agricultural land, not land in housing pipelines, so the mechanism to house-price-to-income is too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar.
